title: Lessons Learned From 100 Hires
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston draws on a department rebuild, about 60 early hires, and then a project that required nearly 100 hires to describe what has improved his hiring. He opens with coaching a youth soccer team, where first impressions proved unreliable, and applies the lesson to hiring: liking a candidate and having evidence they will succeed are different things. His approach replaced traditional interviews for about 90 percent of hires with strict application criteria, a work sample, and three strong references from recent supervisors, and he reports high job satisfaction and roughly 95 percent retention in 2025. He offers ten lessons, including defining the ideal candidate first, screening for competence at the start, standardising reference questions, observing candidates doing the work, using behavioural interview questions, and applying greater rigour to leadership hires. He cites Collins, Adler, and Lencioni throughout. The results are self-reported from one organisation, but the emphasis on evidence over impression is clear and practical.
points: First impressions and interview rapport are weak predictors, so Houston moves evidence of past performance to the front of the process.
A work sample plus three strong references from recent supervisors replaced most traditional interviews in his hiring.
Standardised reference questions on feedback, stress, and conflict help predict interpersonal fit, which he finds harder to fix than skill gaps.
Observing candidates do the work, through paid trials or contract-first arrangements, reveals consistency and judgment better than interviews.
Leadership hires deserve extra rigour because a poor leader hire creates problems for the whole organisation, not just one manager.
quotes: It took time—and repeated observation—to understand each player’s strengths and what I could expect from them. Hiring has taught me the same lesson: first impressions are useful, but they aren’t a reliable predictor of long term performance.

One unusual feature: we did not conduct traditional job interviews for about 90% of those hires. Instead, we relied on strict application criteria, a work sample, and three strong references from recent supervisors.

I still remember applying for a job where the CEO told me, “Parker, I can’t hire you yet. I like you too much.” He explained that he relied on other senior leaders’ assessments and a slow hiring process to keep his own bias in check.
You cannot reliably find what you haven’t clearly defined. Identify the technical and interpersonal competencies the role requires.
Past behavior is the biggest predictor of future behavior. Ask supervisors for specific examples of reliability, judgment, teamwork, and follow-through.
Intelligence and technical ability matter, but they cannot compensate for an unwillingness to learn or an inability to work well with others.
Most people think they are good at hiring but their hiring success is rarely tracked and may only be 50-50. The goal should be to get to 90-10.
